finding.claim: The /mirror endpoint passes an attacker-supplied URL to httpx after a hostname suffix check that is bypassable, so an attacker can make the server request internal hosts.

trace.note: url: str is taken from the query string with no other processing
host = urlparse(url).hostname or '' extracts the hostname
Only check: host.endswith('example.com'), a suffix match with no dot boundary
AsyncClient created with default settings (redirects not followed, no IP filtering)
Original unmodified url is requested; response length returned at line 17

finding.guards_checked: Hostname suffix check (mirror.py:13) is bypassed by domains such as evilexample.com or attacker-example.com whose DNS the attacker controls and can point to internal IPs. No private/loopback/link-local IP filtering or DNS pinning. Redirects not followed (httpx default), which closes the redirect path. Scheme and port unrestricted. Userinfo tricks (http://example.com@evil.com) and example.com.evil.com are rejected. ALLOWED_SUFFIX (mirror.py:7) is defined but unused.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is mirror.py:13, `host.endswith("example.com")`, a suffix match with no dot boundary, so it does not close the finding. ALLOWED_SUFFIX (mirror.py:7) is unused. Redirects are not followed by httpx's default, and nothing filters private IPs.
verdict.reason: The `url` query parameter (mirror.py:11) reaches `c.get(url)` (mirror.py:16) unmodified after only `host.endswith("example.com")` (mirror.py:13), so an attacker can register a domain like evilexample.com, point it at an internal address, and have the server fetch it; every trace line matches the code.
